transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I guess I came in because I can’t get my mind to stop jumping from one thing to the next. Like, at work in the lab, we have this new partnership, and I keep thinking, okay, what if that means they’re going to cut my position, or decide I’m not useful enough? And then I’ll be looking at my data and suddenly I’m convinced maybe it’s wrong, or I missed something obvious, or I’m going to get blamed for it.

And it doesn’t really stay in one lane. It goes from work to money—like my bills piling up—to my family maybe thinking I’m falling behind compared to where I should be. And then I start thinking I’ve already ruined my chances at grad school somehow, even if I can’t point to one clear thing. It’s just… constant. I feel like my brain is always trying to find the next thing that might go wrong.
Did these worries start after a specific stressful event or change in your life?

Yeah… I think there was a pretty clear shift, or at least that’s when it really started feeling like this. It’s been about seven months now. Around the time the lab’s funding changed and they brought in this commercial partnership, everything about how the place was being run started feeling different—less predictable, more like people were making decisions somewhere above me and I couldn’t tell what they meant for my job or for the work.

I don’t know if I can say it was one single day where it started, but that period is when my worrying really ramped up and just kind of… stayed. Since then it’s felt like I haven’t been able to get back to normal.
When the worrying starts, do you feel able to stop or control it?

Not really, no. I mean, I try to. I’ll literally tell myself, like, “Just focus on the one thing in front of you. Finish the report. Check the assay. Read the numbers and move on.” But it doesn’t stay contained like that.

It’s like one worry catches on another one. I’ll be looking at the screen, trying to write something straightforward, and suddenly I’m not really reading anymore—I’m just sitting there while my head is running through every possible way something could go wrong. Like if I make one mistake, then that means the whole thing is off, then someone notices, then it becomes this bigger problem. And even when part of me knows I’m spiraling, I can’t really shut it off. I can redirect for maybe a minute, but then it comes right back.
If the situation at the lab were resolved, do you think your worrying would mostly go back to normal?

I don’t think so, honestly. I mean, the lab situation is definitely a big part of it, and it’s kind of the thing my mind grabs onto first a lot of the time—like whether this new partnership means they’re going to cut my position, or decide I’m not needed, or whether some mistake in my data is going to turn into this huge issue.

But it’s not only that anymore. Even if someone came in tomorrow and said, “Your job is completely safe and the lab is fine,” I feel like my brain would just… move to the next thing. It would go to my bills, or whether I’m falling behind compared to what my family expects, or whether I’ve already messed up my chances at grad school somehow. It’s like the topic changes, but the worrying itself doesn’t really stop.
Has this worrying been interfering with your work or daily life?

Yeah. It has, more than I wanted to admit at first.

At work it’s been the most obvious. I actually missed an internal lab deadline recently, and that’s not really like me. It wasn’t because I didn’t care or because I didn’t have the information — I had the data, I had the pieces — but I just could not organize myself enough to get the writing and the data review done in a clean way. I kept going back over things, second-guessing what I’d written, checking numbers again, then realizing I’d spent all this time and still hadn’t actually finished the report. It felt like my brain was busy the whole time but I wasn’t producing anything useful.

And it’s started spilling into normal life too. Stuff that used to feel manageable now feels like this huge list I’m already behind on. Preparing routine reports feels overwhelming. Showing up to art nights — which used to be something I looked forward to — now feels like another thing I might fail at or not have energy for. Even cooking for my family, which shouldn’t be that complicated, can feel like too much to keep up with. I’ll think about what needs to be done and it’s like everything piles up at once, so I either put it off or I do it while feeling completely tense the whole time.

So, yeah, it’s definitely interfering. It’s not just thoughts in the background anymore. It’s affecting what I actually get done.
Have you been feeling restless or on edge a lot of the time?

Yeah, a lot. It’s not even just mentally on edge, it’s like my body is wound up too.

At work especially, I’ll sit down at my desk and I just can’t really settle into the chair. I’ll be trying to focus, but my leg is bouncing under the bench, or I’m tapping my foot, or shifting around like I’m uncomfortable even if nothing is actually wrong with the chair or the room. I catch myself checking messages over and over, not because I’m expecting anything specific, but because I feel like I need to do something.

And I keep getting up for no real reason. Like I’ll walk back to the instrument room even though I was just there, or I’ll go check something that doesn’t actually need checking, just because sitting still feels impossible. Even normal lab sounds — someone shutting a drawer, a machine clicking, a cart moving — make me jump sometimes, which is embarrassing because it’s not like anything dangerous happened. I’m just already so keyed up that everything feels like it hits me too hard.
Aside from the lab changes, have these worries also been happening in areas of your life that are unrelated to that stress?

Yes, definitely. I mean, the lab stuff is kind of the loudest worry right now, because it’s right in front of me every day, but it’s not contained there at all.

That’s actually why I came in, because my mind is constantly jumping around. One minute I’m thinking about whether this new partnership at the lab means they’re going to cut my position, and then it turns into, “What if my data are wrong and I missed something obvious?” But then even when I’m not at work, it keeps going. I’ll start thinking about bills and whether they’re going to pile up, or whether my family thinks I’m falling behind compared to where I should be at 24, or whether I’ve already messed up my chances at grad school somehow.

It’s like the subject changes, but the feeling is the same. I can’t just tell myself, “Okay, that’s a work problem, leave it at work,” because my brain just finds another thing to latch onto.
Have these constant worries been happening on most days for at least six months?

Yeah… I’d say yes. It’s been about seven months now, if I’m counting from when things changed at the lab — when the funding shifted and that commercial partnership started changing how everything was being run.

At first I kept thinking it was just a temporary reaction, like, “Okay, things are unstable, anyone would be stressed.” But it didn’t really settle down. It’s been there most days since then, just kind of following me around. Some days it’s louder than others, but I don’t think there have been many days where I felt genuinely free of it.
Do you feel your level of worry is stronger than would be expected for what’s actually happening in your life right now?

Yeah… honestly, I think it is stronger than what’s actually going on, even though it doesn’t feel that way in the moment.

Like, there are real things happening — the lab partnership, the funding stuff, all of that — so I keep using that as proof that I’m being rational. But then my mind just takes it way beyond the actual facts. I came in because it’s not just, “Oh, work is uncertain.” It’s like my brain immediately jumps from, “What if this new partnership means they cut my position?” to “What if my data are wrong and I missed something obvious?” and then to bills piling up, and then to whether my family thinks I’m falling behind, and then to whether I’ve already ruined my chances at grad school.

It’s like I can’t keep the worry proportional. One concern turns into five other concerns, and they all feel urgent, even if nothing has actually happened yet. So yeah, I think if I step back, the amount of worry is probably much bigger than what the situation calls for.
Have you been having a lot of muscle tension?

Yeah, a lot. It’s actually one of the things I notice physically the most.

My shoulders and neck are just… tight almost all day, like they’re stuck up near my ears without me realizing it. I’ll be sitting at my computer going through spreadsheets or checking data, and then I suddenly notice I’m clenching my jaw really hard, like my teeth are pressed together for no reason. I don’t even catch myself doing it until my face or neck starts to feel sore.

By the evening it feels like I’ve been hauling equipment around all day, even if I’ve mostly just been sitting. My neck gets stiff, my shoulders ache, and I’ll get these headaches that feel like they’re coming from the tension. It’s not just “I’m a little stressed” tightness — it feels like my body has been bracing for something all day.
Do these worries feel mainly centered on the changes at the lab?

Not mainly, no… I mean, the lab changes are kind of where it starts a lot of the time, because that’s the obvious thing in front of me. Like I’ll think, “What if this new partnership means they cut my position?” and then I can’t just leave it there.

It sort of spreads out from that. Then I’m worrying whether my data are wrong, like maybe I missed something basic and everyone’s going to realize it. Then I start thinking about money and bills piling up if things go badly. Then it turns into whether my family thinks I’m falling behind, and whether I’ve already messed up my chances at grad school somehow.

So the lab is a big trigger, definitely, but it doesn’t stay contained there. My mind keeps jumping from one thing to the next until it feels like my whole life is on the line.
Before the changes at the lab, were you already someone who worried a lot about different parts of life?

Not really in the same way. I mean, I’ve always been someone who thinks things through maybe more than some people, but this level of worrying didn’t really start until about seven months ago, when the funding shift happened and the commercial partnership changed how everything at the lab was being run.

That was sort of the turning point. Before that, I could get stressed about school or work or family stuff, sure, but it didn’t feel like my mind was constantly branching out into every possible bad outcome. Since the lab changes, it’s like the uncertainty there set something off, and now it spreads into all these other areas instead of staying just about work. So… yeah, about seven months, and it’s been pretty steady since then.
Has the worrying continued for more than six months since the changes at the lab began?

Yes — it’s been more than six months. I’d say about seven months now, starting around when the lab’s funding shifted and that commercial partnership changed how everything was being run.

At first I thought it was just a temporary reaction, like, okay, things are unstable at work and I’m just stressed because nobody really knows what’s happening. But it didn’t settle down after a few weeks. It just kept going, and now looking back, it’s basically been steady since then. So yeah… about seven months.
If the uncertainty at the lab had never happened, do you think you would still be dealing with this level of anxiety?

I honestly don’t know. I’ve thought about that a lot, actually, because part of me wants to say, “No, if the lab hadn’t changed, I’d probably be fine,” because that really did feel like the thing that kicked all of this off.

But I also don’t know if it just… exposed something that was already there? Like maybe I was always prone to getting stuck in my head, and this was just the first situation that was uncertain enough and important enough that I couldn’t manage it the usual way. It’s hard to separate that out, because I can’t really rewind and test it.

I think without the lab uncertainty, I probably wouldn’t be at this level. Or at least I don’t think it would have gotten this intense. But I’m not completely sure, because now that it’s happening, it feels like it’s attached to everything, not just the lab. So… I guess my answer is I don’t know for sure, but I suspect the lab situation was the main thing that set it off.
Do you feel your anxiety is mainly a reaction to the changes at the lab?

I think it started as a reaction to the lab changes, yeah. That’s still the center of it in a lot of ways — like whether this new partnership means my position gets cut, or whether the priorities are going to shift and I won’t have a place there anymore.

But it doesn’t stay neatly contained there. That’s the problem. My mind jumps from that to, okay, what if my data are wrong, what if I’ve missed something obvious, what if this affects my future in the field. Then suddenly I’m thinking about bills piling up, and whether my family thinks I’m falling behind, and whether I’ve already messed up my chances at grad school.

So… yes, the lab changes feel like the thing that set it off, but now the anxiety is bigger than just that one situation. It’s like the lab uncertainty opened the door, and now everything feels like something I can worry myself into a corner about.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, honestly. I mean, I know my sleep hasn’t felt great, but I haven’t really tracked it or anything, so I don’t want to say something too definite and make it sound more precise than it is.

Some nights I get into bed and I’m just… aware that I’m not settling quickly, but I don’t know if that counts as “trouble sleeping” in the way you mean. And then other nights I think I sleep, but I still wake up feeling like I didn’t really rest. But again, I haven’t been keeping times or anything like that, so it’s hard for me to separate what’s actually happening from what I’m just worried about happening.

So I guess the honest answer is: maybe, but I’m not completely sure. I’ve noticed sleep feels off, but I don’t have a clear pattern I can point to.
Do you feel the anxiety would go away if the situation at the lab were fully resolved?

I want to say yes, because it would be such a relief if the lab situation were just settled — like if someone could tell me clearly whether my position is safe or not, and what the new partnership actually means. I think that would take away a huge chunk of it.

But I don’t know if it would make the anxiety go away completely, because at this point it’s not only the lab anymore. That’s why I came in, really. My mind keeps jumping from, “What if this partnership means they cut my position?” to “What if my data are wrong?” or “What if I missed something obvious?” And then somehow I’m already thinking about bills piling up, or whether my family thinks I’m falling behind, or whether I’ve already ruined my chances at grad school.

So… if the lab were fully resolved, I think I’d probably feel better, maybe a lot better. But I’m worried my brain would just find the next thing to latch onto. It’s like the lab is the main trigger, but the worrying has spread into everything else.
Do you feel your anxiety has been out of proportion to what most people would feel about the changes at the lab?

Yeah… I think so. I don’t want to dismiss the fact that the lab changes are genuinely stressful — I mean, I think most people in my position would be worried if a new partnership might affect their job or role. So part of me keeps trying to tell myself, “This is reasonable, this is what anyone would feel.”

But then the way my mind handles it feels… bigger than that. It doesn’t just stop at, “I hope my position doesn’t get cut.” It turns into this constant chain where I’m thinking about whether the partnership means I’m out, and then I’m thinking, what if my data are wrong, what if I’ve missed something obvious, what if this makes me look incompetent, and then suddenly I’m not even just at the lab anymore — I’m thinking about bills piling up, or my family thinking I’m falling behind, or whether I’ve already ruined my chances at grad school.

So I guess, yes, it feels out of proportion in the sense that I can’t contain it. I don’t think the situation is nothing, but my reaction feels like it keeps expanding past what’s actually happening.
During the past seven months, has there been a period when the lab situation felt less stressful but the excessive worrying still continued?

Yeah… I think there have been times when the lab situation was quieter, or at least not actively blowing up that day, and the worry still didn’t really stop.

Like, even if there wasn’t a new email about the partnership or no one had said anything new about positions being cut, my mind would just keep going. It would start with the lab — like, “What if this still means I lose my position?” — but then it would slide into other things really fast. I’d be thinking, “What if my data are wrong?” or “What if I missed something obvious and everyone finds out I’m not as competent as they think?” And then somehow it’s not even just work anymore, it’s bills, and whether I’m falling behind compared to where I’m supposed to be, and whether my family thinks I’m messing up, and whether I’ve already ruined my chances at grad school.

So yes, I guess that’s part of what scares me. Even when the lab stress is less immediate, the worrying keeps finding something else to attach to. It doesn’t feel like it just turns off when that one situation calms down.
Have you felt this anxiety mainly because of the changes at the lab?

Mostly, yes, the lab changes are what started it and they’re still the thing my mind comes back to the most. Like, the new partnership and not knowing whether my position might get cut — that’s the main spark, I think.

But it doesn’t stay there. That’s kind of why I came in. My mind keeps jumping from, “What if this partnership means I’m out?” to, “What if my data are wrong?” or “What if I missed something obvious?” And then before I know it, I’m worrying about bills piling up, or my family thinking I’m falling behind, or whether I’ve already messed up my chances at grad school.

So I’d say it’s mainly because of the lab in the sense that that’s the center of it, but the anxiety doesn’t feel contained to that anymore. It feels like once it starts, it spreads into everything else.
